newsitem.title: Norway: Nobel Peace Prize winners in separate peace calls.
newsitem.headline: Nobel Peace Prize winners in separate peace calls.

text.p: East Timor Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo and resistance leader Jose Ramos Horta, co-winners of the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize, appealed on Monday to Jakarta for a dialogue on a peace settlement in the Indonesia-ruled territory.

However, they called for dialogue at separate news conferences at the Norwegian Nobel Institute in what Ramos Horta hinted was a result of pressure by the Jakarta government on Belo, who will share the prize on Tuesday with the self-exiled activist.
"As a religious leader, I am ready to collaborate with everybody who are really committed to efforts for peace and justice in East Timor," the bishop said.

Ramos Horta, at a follow-on news conference, said: "We are willing, open to engage in a dialogue with Indonesia without preconditions, in the framework of the United Nations in the search for a solution to the problems of East Timor."
Nobel Committee officials said the laureates -- one a religious leader, the other a political leader -- held separate news conferences at their own request, but Ramos Horta said:
"I certainly would have preferred a joint press conference with Bishop Belo. It is obvious why this is not the case."
Indonesia has condemned the inclusion of Ramos Horta with Belo as a Peace Prize winner and has said it will not be represented at the award ceremony in the Norwegian capital.

Nobel Institute chairman Francis Sejersted, asked if the Indonesian government had told Belo not to meet media jointly with Ramos Horta, said: "I don't know. The Indonesian government has obviously been very active in many ways."
He did not elaborate but Indonesian ambassador Aminruddin Noor dismissed suggestions that attempts to influence Belo had been made.
"I would categorically again deny that there is any Indonesian embassy people here, who would talk to him to stop him from saying things," Noor told Norwegian television.

In October, the Nobel Committee announced it would award the prestigious $1.12 million prize jointly to Ramos Horta, who has led resistance in the territory to its annexation by Indonesia, and Belo, who has championed human rights.

Many East Timorese resent the rule of Indonesia, which annexed the former Portuguese colony in 1976 following an armed invasion the previous year. The United Nations continues to reject Indonesian claims to sovereignty and considers Portugal the administering power.
Belo sought to play down the fact that he and Ramos Horta did not attend a joint news conference. "The fact that we are not here together is not a problem," he said.

But the bishop, who has defended his parishioners against human rights violations by the Indonesian military, dodged all political questions: "I am a religious leader. Leave the political issues to the politicians, please."

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas warned Belo last month against meddling in politics after an interview in which the German magazine Der Spiegel quoted him as saying Indonesian troops treated East Timorese like "scabby dogs" and "slaves".
Belo has said he was misquoted.
"I understand his role, his difficulties," Ramos Horta said. "He is much more needed in East Timor than I am. He is desperately needed by the people. He has to go back.
"Therefore I believe it is wise for Bishop Belo not to be with me in this press conference."
